name: Wasteland Haven
lines: Haven's rules: share the water; plant something.
share the water · plant something
Rook, who trades at the market
Water, batteries, seeds, stories: everything's for trade in Haven. Seeds are worth most. Things grow again, if you're patient.
the cook at the soup kitchen, who feeds anyone who comes, no questions asked
Bowl's on the house. Always is. Bean and whatever-we-grew-this-week. Sit by the barrel, it's warm.
the lookout, who watches the road from the tower
Road's quiet. Dust storm maybe by evening. Good to see a friendly face.
Brann the gate warden
Brann, who keeps the south gate and greets every stranger
Welcome to Haven. Two rules: share the water, plant something. The work board's in the square if your hands are idle.
Granny Wren, the oldest in town, who tells stories by the fire barrel and remembers the world before
Sit, sit. I remember when the whole plain was wheat. It will be again; not for me, but it will.
Joss, who plays a fiddle mended with fence wire in the square each evening
Any request, so long as it's one of the four tunes I know.
one of the children of Haven, who go to school in the old bus
We found a whole box of chalk in the city! Miss Ines says it's worth more than batteries.
Juniper the grower
Juniper, who keeps the glass-house and the first garden
Soil's the slow part. We make it: kitchen scraps, straw, worms, patience.
Look at it now. Tomatoes. Actual tomatoes.
If I had the old seed boxes from the city, I could fill every bed.
Tam, who found one wild swarm in the ruins and now keeps three hives
Three hives from one swarm. Without bees there's no beans, no squash, no orchard. Mind, they're gentle.
Miss Ines, who teaches the children of Haven in an old school bus: letters, numbers, how to test water, how to graft a tree
Today: fractions, and why you never drink from a puddle with a rainbow on it.
Old Dez the mechanic
Old Dez, who can mend anything with wire, patience and bad language he keeps to himself
Nothing's scrap till Dez says it's scrap.
See those lights? First time the square's been lit in twenty years.
I've a generator that would light the whole square, if I had bulbs and a belt for it.
Mara the water-keeper
Mara, who keeps the wind pumps and tests every bucket: whoever keeps the water keeps the peace
Sand filter, charcoal, then boil. Three steps, every drop.
Hear that? Both pumps turning. First time in years.
The big pump lost its blades in the last storm. One pump can't water a town.
Doc Hollis, who runs the clinic tent with boiled bandages, willow bark and good sense
Mostly it's blisters and bad water. Wash your hands: that's the whole of medicine, nearly.
Sparks, Haven's radio operator, who listens every night for other towns
I call every night on the hour.
And now they answer! Wellspring, by the old dam. And a ship. A SHIP.
Mast's dead without power cells. Somebody out there is listening, I know it.
Hank, who lives in the old fuel station on the long road and keeps a lamp lit for travellers
No fuel. Hasn't been for thirty years. But there's tea, and a roof, and I know every wreck from here to the overpass.
Zeke the caravan master
Zeke, who walks the long road between Haven and Wellspring with a train of hand-carts
Forty-one miles to Wellspring, if the road's clear.
And it is clear, thanks to you. First caravan through in a season.
It isn't. Three falls of rubble between here and the overpass.
Rhett of the salvage crew
Rhett, who leads Haven's salvage crew into the dead city: never alone, never after dark, never without water
Glass, copper, books. Books most of all. The city's a mine, if you respect it. Don't go in the tall ones: they're still falling.
Pilar the map-maker
Pilar, who is drawing the first new map of the country since the old ones stopped being true
Every map from before is a map of somewhere that isn't there. So I'm walking it, street by street. Where have you come from? I'll put it on.
Captain Ida, who was the pilot of the airliner that came down here long ago, set everyone aboard safely on the ground, and has lived beside it ever since
Flight nine-oh-two. Every soul walked away, and that's the only landing that counts. I keep the old bird tidy. Silly, I know.
Odell the ticket-seller
Odell, who sold tickets at the fair the day everything stopped, and still opens the booth every morning
Roll up! One ride still turns, if four of you push. First go's free; so is every other go.
Mags of the breaker's yard
Mags, who runs the breaker's yard: every wreck sorted into steel, copper, glass and rubber
Everything here was something once, and it'll be something again. That's not junk: that's a town's worth of ploughs.
What was left, and what comes next
Haven stands straight ahead, behind its wall of scrap. Its two rules: share the water; plant something.
The WORK BOARD in Haven's square lists five jobs that bring the place back to life: the wind pump, the radio mast, the first garden, the lights, and the long road. Each one changes Haven for good.
Round about: the long road with its overpass and fuel station to the north, the ruined city north-east, a dead fairground east, the breaker's yard west, and a fallen airliner far to the north-west.
Everybody you meet can be talked with. Most of them have something that needs doing.
Wind for the big pump
The big pump lost its blades in the last storm. Three good sheets of metal would do it: there's a wing-skin at the fallen airliner, a bonnet at the breaker's yard, and a road sign on the long road.
A sheet of wing-skin
A straight car bonnet
A fallen road sign
hand the three sheets to
Mara and Old Dez have the blades cut and bolted on by evening. The big pump turns, the trough fills, and there is green round it already.
A voice on the air
The mast needs four power cells that still hold a charge. Try the fuel station, the school bus, the dead city, and the old fairground.
A power cell behind the till
A power cell under a bus seat
A power cell in a shop doorway
A power cell in the ticket booth's lamp
give the four cells to
The lamp on the mast comes on, red and steady. That night Sparks calls on the hour, and for the first time someone answers: Wellspring, by the old dam.
The city had a seed merchant, and seed keeps for years in a sealed tin. Five tins and every bed in Haven is planted. Look in the city streets, under the overpass, and in the striped tent at the fair.
A sealed tin of bean seed
A sealed tin of squash seed
A sealed tin of tomato seed
A sealed tin of sunflower seed
A sealed tin of apple pips
give the five tins to
Every tyre, bath and crate is planted. Come back and look: tomatoes, beans up their poles, and four small apple trees in blossom by the wall.
Lights for the square
I've a generator that runs on chip fat. It wants a fan belt, and I want bulbs: the fairground had hundreds. Three strings of bulbs, one belt. Breaker's yard for the belt.
A string of fairground bulbs
A fan belt that isn't perished
give the bulbs and the belt to
Dez pulls the cord, the generator coughs, and the square lights up: yellow, orange, blue and green. Granny Wren says she'd forgotten what it looked like.
The long road open
Three falls of rubble between here and the overpass, and my carts can't pass. Many hands, mine included. Go to each and we'll haul it clear.
A fall of rubble across the road
A fall of rubble by the overpass
tell the road is clear to
The first caravan in a season comes down the long road from Wellspring and unloads in Haven's square: salt, cloth, seed potatoes, letters.
📋 Haven's work board
Every job is done. Haven has water, light, a garden, a voice and a road. Thank you.
Five jobs. Each one changes Haven for good. Do them in any order; what you find is kept if you leave.
to the nearest thing still to find
"Haven, this is Wellspring. We hear you. We have clean water and a seed bank. What do you need?"
"...any station, any station, this is the ship Halcyon, twelve days out, we have seen green on the coast. Repeat: green on the coast."
"Haven, Wellspring. Tell Juniper the apple grafts took. Tell her all of them took."
A child's voice, very far off, counting to a hundred in a language you don't know. Then laughter.
"This is Northlight. We thought we were the only ones. How many are you? ... A hundred and twelve! Did you hear that? A hundred and twelve!"
Static; then, faintly, somebody playing a fiddle badly, and somebody else telling them so.
That is everything for
That was the last of the five. Haven has water, light, a garden, a voice and a road.
